newsitem.title: UK: Hume challenges London and IRA on N.Irish peace.
newsitem.headline: Hume challenges London and IRA on N.Irish peace.

text.p: John Hume, a Catholic nationalist leader in Northern Ireland, said on Saturday Britain could pave the way for a new IRA truce by clearly stating it wants genuine all-party talks aimed at quick progress on decades of strife.

A key figure in efforts to salvage the province's battered peace process, Hume called on the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to recognise a widespread yearning for peace and proclaim a truce that would get their Sinn Fein political arm into talks.

In a keynote address to his party's annual conference, Hume said all sides must work to restore an IRA truce so that current multi-party talks take place in a peaceful climate, with Sinn Fein being given a seat for the first time.

"I believe that Prime Minister John Major wants to see that happen, that he wants to achieve lasting peace in our country and that his government can achieve it by reiterating in the clearest possible terms the nature, objectives and time-frame of the talks, together with confidence-building measures that can improve the atmosphere of the talks themselves," Hume said.

Hume, whose Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) speaks for most of the province's 40 percent Irish Catholic minority, urged the IRA to banish distrust of Britain. He said a 17-month ceasefire that ended in February had transformed the mood of people in both parts of the partitioned island.

"I ask the IRA to renew their ceasefire and create the circumstances where all the energies of all our people are devoted to building a new Ireland based on respect for both of our traditions". Britain and Ireland, joint sponsors of multi-party talks that began in June, say Sinn Fein will not be admitted until the IRA calls an end to its war against British rule.

Republicans say the IRA will not call a new ceasefire if they believe Britain's Protestant "Unionist" supporters in Northern Ireland will be allowed to dominate proceedings, with demands for a prior handover of guerrilla arms.
Wrangling over the "arms decommissioning" question has blighted political momentum for many months.

Hume said that setting "a time-frame" would concentrate the minds of the rival parties. "I am not advocating a political "sell by' or perhaps a "settle by' date, after which the process is binned," he said.
The guerrillas resumed hostilities in February this year, accusing London of reneging on a deal offering a place in talks as a reward for the original truce declared in September 1994.
Hume said it was a tragedy that Sinn Fein had not been given a seat at the conference table after the first ceasefire.

"Historians will judge the reasons for the delay by the British government in starting the all-party talks but it is my own strong conviction that, had they started soon after the ceasefire, that we would have lasting peace by now."
